extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of dramatic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing, staging, and wording a tragic drama: how to build plot (recognition, reversal, complication/unravelling), shape episodes, integrate chorus and action, and use diction and metaphor to produce tragic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis): preferred types
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition may arise by different means (false inference, tokens/amulets, reasoning), but of all recognitions the best is that which arises from the incidents themselves—the startling discovery made by natural means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that emerge naturally from the plot (e.g., Oedipus, Iphigenia) and avoid artificial devices (tokens or amulets). Next-best are recognitions produced by process of reasoning. Beware of contrived recognitions based on false inference by characters unless the false inference is integral and plausible in the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualizing the scene (vivid staging in the poet's mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing the plot and working it out with proper diction, the poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes so he sees everything with utmost vividness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualizing the situation helps discover what is in keeping with it and avoids overlooking inconsistencies; failing to do so can offend an audience (example: Carcinus). Use this mental staging to check plausibility and continuity of events and gestures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate gesture and delivery planning
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should work out his play, to the best of his power, with appropriate gestures; actors who feel emotion are most convincing through natural sympathy with their characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan physical actions and gestures that suit the emotion and situation so that actors can evoke natural sympathy. Casting and directing should aim for performers who can inhabit emotional states (either by natural gift or an intense commitment) to produce lifelike reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic emotional expression by actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who feel emotion are most convincing—one who is agitated storms, one who is angry rages—so that poetry implies either a happy gift of nature or a strain of madness enabling realistic portrayals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor performers able to convey genuine feeling; avoid unemotional or artificial delivery that undermines the audience's sympathy. The poet/director should shape roles to permit authentic affective expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story construction: outline then detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the poet takes a story ready-made or constructs it, he should first sketch its general outline, and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the skeleton of the plot (essential situations and turning points), then add episodes that serve the main action. Use examples like Iphigenia to test whether incidental elements (e.g., oracles, journeys) fit the plot's core purpose rather than being arbitrary additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and brevity of episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: After giving the general plan, it remains to fill in the episodes; we must see that they are relevant to the action. In drama the episodes are short, and it is these that give extension to epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include episodes that advance or illuminate the central action; trim extraneous material. Avoid lengthy episodic expansions appropriate to epic but harmful to dramatic unity—keep episodes concise and directly tied to the plot's stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic structure: Complication and Unravelling (denouement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts—Complication and Unravelling. The Complication extends from the beginning of the action to the turning-point to good or bad fortune; the Unravelling extends from the beginning of the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the plot so the turning-point (reversal) is clear and the Unravelling resolves consequences logically. Ensure the Complication accumulates causes that make the reversal believable and the Unravelling satisfactorily resolves the moral/plot consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of tragedy and poetic elements to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of Tragedy: the Complex (depending on Reversal and Recognition), the Pathetic (motive is passion), the Ethical (motives are ethical), and the Simple. The poet should endeavour, if possible, to combine all poetic elements, or failing that, the greatest number and the most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to blend reversal/recognition, ethical motives, and pathos where feasible; if constrained, prioritize the elements most essential to the intended tragic effect. Recognize which kind your work aligns with and shape plot and characterization accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epic multiplicity of plots in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should remember not to make an Epic structure into a Tragedy—i.e., avoid a multiplicity of plots (as in dramatizing the whole Iliad); in drama each part must assume proper magnitude, and multiplying plots leads to failure or poor success on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a portion or episode of a larger tale rather than dramatising an entire epic narrative. Focus on a single dominant plotline with tightly connected episodes to preserve dramatic unity and stage effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot identity as test of sameness/difference
rubrics_metrics.description: In speaking of a tragedy as the same or different, the best test is the plot: identity exists where the Complication and Unravelling are the same. Many poets tie the knot well but unravel it ill—both arts should be mastered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing works (or adapting), evaluate whether complication + unravelling coincide. Ensure both the construction of the knot (Complication) and its resolution (Unravelling) are handled with equal skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of the Chorus into the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole and share in the action (in the manner of Sophocles), not serve as mere choral interludes as in later poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chorus to advance or comment on the action in a unified way; avoid inserting choral songs that are irrelevant or interchangeable between plays (an anti-pattern attributed to Agathon and later poets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (ideas) in drama: aims and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (more at home in Rhetoric) includes every effect to be produced by speech: proof and refutation, the excitation of feelings (pity, fear, anger), suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting speeches, focus on the rhetorical effects desired (persuasion, incitement of emotion, irony). Ensure that speech-produced effects complement the incidents; speeches should not reveal Thought apart from what is said but should be the means to produce Thought's effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents should speak for themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic incidents must be treated like dramatic speeches when aiming to evoke pity, fear, importance, or probability; the incidents should speak for themselves without verbal exposition, while speeches must produce the effects by the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show rather than tell—arrange actions so they carry semantic and emotional weight without needing overt explanation. Avoid expository scenes that explain what well-constructed incidents could demonstrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of utterance and division of craft (diction vs delivery)
rubrics_metrics.description: One branch of inquiry treats the Modes of Utterance (what is a command, a prayer, a statement, a threat, a question, an answer); this province belongs to the art of Delivery rather than poetry itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should be aware of modes but understand that practical execution (intonation, delivery) is largely the responsibility of actors/directors. Do not censure a playwright for fine points of delivery outside the poet's craft, but plan utterance types to enable effective delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and lexical choices (words, metaphor, style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be simple, compound, current, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, newly-coined, lengthened, contracted, or altered. Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference (genus↔species, species↔genus, species↔species, or analogy); metaphors can be qualified by adding the relative term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words appropriate to the audience and effect (current vs strange). Use metaphors formed by transference or analogy to enrich diction; when a metaphor risks obscurity, qualify it by indicating the relative term. Avoid gratuitous archaisms or foreign words that obscure meaning unless effect requires them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonology and prosodic awareness for diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Language comprises letters, syllables, connecting words, nouns, verbs, inflexions, and sentences; knowledge of these (e.g., vowel, semi-vowel, mute distinctions) matters for metre and delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of sound properties (long/short, aspiration, accents) insofar as they affect rhythm and oral performance. While metrical detail is for metre-writers, playwrights should consider sound and syllabic shape when composing lines meant for recitation.
